title.en: History: Colonialism in Asia and Africa

text.en: Raju found Africa on the world map, divided into many straight-edged countries. "Why so straight?" he asked.

Colonialism means one country ruling and using another. European powers like Britain, France, Portugal, Spain and the Netherlands built colonies in Asia and Africa to get raw materials and markets. The Scramble for Africa saw them divide the continent at the Berlin Conference of 1884.
In Asia, Britain ruled India, the Dutch ruled Indonesia, and the French ruled Indo-China. Colonial rule drained wealth, changed farming and harmed local industries, but it also brought railways and new ideas.
People resisted through revolts and later national movements, and most colonies became free in the 20th century.

The Scramble for Africa saw them divide the continent at the Berlin Conference of 1884.
In Asia, Britain ruled India, the Dutch ruled Indonesia, and the French ruled Indo-China.

Colonialism is the practice where a stronger power conquers and rules another land, exploiting its raw materials, labour and markets. Imperialism describes the broader drive to build overseas empires.
Why did European powers race for colonies in the nineteenth century? Industrial factories craved cheap cotton, rubber, tin, palm oil and gold, plus captive overseas markets to sell finished goods.

board.text: Economic motive: raw materials & captive markets

text.en: Alongside profit came fierce national rivalry among Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Portugal—each claiming prestige from the size of its empire.
In Asia, the British East India Company shifted from trader to ruler after the Battle of Plassey (1757) and Battle of Buxar (1764), gradually bringing most of India under British control.
Colonial land-revenue systems—Permanent Settlement in Bengal, Ryotwari in Madras and Mahalwari in northern India—extracted heavy taxes that pushed peasants into debt and famines.
Indian nationalist Dadabhai Naoroji exposed the 'Drain of Wealth'—showing how India's taxes and trade surplus were siphoned off to Britain instead of building Indian schools or industry.
Elsewhere in Asia, the Dutch controlled Indonesia (the Dutch East Indies) for spices and rubber, France colonised Indo-China (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia), and Britain took Burma and Malaya.

board.text: Colonial Asia: Dutch Indonesia, French Indo-China, British Burma

text.en: China was never formally partitioned into a single colony, yet after the Opium Wars (1839–42) Western powers forced unequal treaties and carved 'spheres of influence' along its coast.

board.text: China: Opium Wars & spheres of influence

text.en: Japan followed a different path: after the Meiji Restoration of 1868, Japan modernised rapidly, avoided Western colonisation, and became an industrial power itself.

Now turn to Africa. Until the 1870s, Europeans held mostly coastal trading posts, while the interior remained independent. Then steamboats, quinine against malaria and machine guns triggered the 'Scramble for Africa'.
At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, European powers drew straight borders across the map of Africa without inviting a single African leader—splitting ethnic groups and uniting rivals arbitrarily.

board.text: Berlin Conference (1884–85): Africa carved on a map

text.en: King Leopold II of Belgium turned the Congo into a brutal personal estate for rubber and ivory, while Britain sought a 'Cape to Cairo' corridor and France controlled vast West and North African lands.
In South Africa, Dutch-descended Boers and British settlers clashed in the Boer War over gold and diamonds, while native Africans were stripped of land and later subjected to racial apartheid.

board.text: South Africa: gold, Boer War & racial segregation

text.en: Two African nations famously resisted European conquest during the Scramble: Ethiopia, which defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa (1896), and Liberia.

Colonialism also caused the forced migration of millions of Africans through the earlier Transatlantic Slave Trade and later Indian indentured labourers sent to plantations in Fiji, Mauritius, Malaya and South Africa.
Across both Asia and Africa, colonial rule reshaped economies into export-only plantations and mines, neglecting local food crops, rural healthcare and mass literacy.

board.text: Plantation & mine economies neglected local welfare

text.en: Yet colonial rule also sparked powerful anti-colonial nationalism. Modern press, railways, Western-educated reformers and mass movements united people to demand self-rule.
In India, resistance grew from early revolts like 1857 to the Indian National Congress and Mahatma Gandhi's mass non-violent struggle, winning independence in 1947.

India's independence inspired a wave of decolonisation across Asia and Africa through the 1950s and 1960s, led by figures like Kwame Nkrumah in Ghana, Ho Chi Minh in Vietnam and Nelson Mandela in South Africa.
Even after independence, newly freed nations faced artificial borders, depleted treasuries and uneven global trade—challenges they addressed through Non-Alignment and national development plans.
Notice the link with the previous chapter: the Industrial Revolution created the factories, weapons and hunger for raw materials that drove nineteenth-century colonialism.
Compare India and Africa: both lost raw wealth and political freedom, yet both built resilient freedom struggles that transformed the twentieth-century world.
Key milestones: 1757 Plassey -> 1839 Opium War -> 1884–85 Berlin Conference -> 1896 Battle of Adwa -> 1947 Indian Independence.
Studying colonialism reminds us why national sovereignty, fair international trade and respect for every people's self-determination are precious.

board.text: Sovereignty & fair trade matter to every nation

problem.en: Why did the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 leave lasting political problems for African nations even after independence?

text.en: Look at who drew Africa's borders.

why.en: European diplomats drew straight-line colonial borders in Berlin without consulting African communities.

text.en: See how those borders affected people.

why.en: Single ethnic and linguistic groups were split across rival colonies, while historically distinct groups were forced into one territory.

text.en: Connect to post-independence challenges.

why.en: When African countries won freedom decades later, they inherited those artificial borders, requiring careful nation-building to maintain unity.

prompt.en: A friend says The Berlin Conference gave Africa its freedom. How will you reply?

points.en: Colonialism is rule over another land.
